descripcion_es: Parts of the body, symptoms, going to the doctor and healthy habits.
resumen: Vocabulary to say what hurts, describe symptoms, talk to the doctor or the pharmacist and discuss lifestyle habits.

explicacion.texto: For pain, use have + a + part of the body with -ache (I have a headache) or my … hurts (my back hurts). With parts of the body, English uses the possessive, not the article: I broke my arm, not “the arm”.

filas: parts of the upper body (es: cabeza / cuello / espalda)
parts of the upper limb (es: brazo / mano / dedo)
parts of the lower limb (es: pierna / rodilla / pie, pies)
parts of the trunk (es: estómago / pecho)
I have a pain in my chest.
pain in the head / stomach (es: dolor de cabeza / de estómago)
pain in a tooth / the back (es: dolor de muelas / de espalda)
pain in the throat (es: dolor de garganta)
common illnesses (es: un resfriado / la gripe)
He's in bed with the flu.
to want to vomit / to feel the room spinning (es: tener náuseas / estar mareado)
to cause pain, to damage a part of the body (es: doler, hacerse daño / lesionarse)
I hurt my ankle playing football.
to react badly to something (es: ser alérgico a)
to arrange a time to see someone (es: pedir cita)
I'd like to make an appointment with the doctor.
a doctor's written order for medicine (es: receta médica)
You need a prescription for these pills.
to swallow medicine (es: tomar medicinas / pastillas)
What's the matter? – I feel ill.
to become healthy again (es: mejorar / recuperarse)
I hope you get better soon.
to stay in good physical condition (es: mantenerse en forma / sano)
to stop smoking (es: dejar de fumar)
He gave up smoking last year.
healthy eating with the right mix of foods (es: una dieta equilibrada)

items: Constipated means “estreñido”, not “constipado” (which is have a cold).
In British English, sick usually means wanting to vomit (feel sick); ill means not well.
Recipe is a cooking recipe; the doctor's one is a prescription.

ejemplos.frase: I've had a sore throat since Monday.
ejemplos.traduccion: Me duele la garganta desde el lunes.

ejemplos.frase: You should stay in bed and drink plenty of water.
ejemplos.traduccion: Deberías quedarte en cama y beber mucha agua.

ejemplos.frase: She twisted her ankle while she was running.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se torció el tobillo mientras corría.

ejemplos.frase: The doctor gave me a prescription for antibiotics.
ejemplos.traduccion: El médico me hizo una receta de antibióticos.

ejemplos.frase: I walk to work every day to keep fit.
ejemplos.traduccion: Voy andando al trabajo todos los días para mantenerme en forma.

ejemplos.frase: Are you allergic to any medicine?

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I'm constipated, I have a runny nose.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I've got a cold, I have a runny nose.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Constipated means “estreñido”; “constipado” is have a cold.

errores_hispanohablantes.bien: My head hurts. / I have a headache.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: English uses the possessive and the verb hurt with no object.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The doctor gave me a recipe.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The doctor gave me a prescription.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With parts of the body, use the possessive instead of the article.

ejercicios.frase: I can't eat anything. I've got terrible ___ (dolor de muelas).
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule from Rules and key points: pains are formed with the part of the body + -ache (headache, stomachache, toothache, backache). The clue is the gloss “dolor de muelas” and the context of not being able to eat. Tooth + ache gives toothache, written as one word. With toothache the article can be left out, as in the example in the card “She has toothache”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Pain in a tooth is toothache.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puedo comer nada. Tengo un dolor de muelas terrible.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Compounds use the singular: toothache, even if several teeth hurt.
It is understandable, but it is not the word the card asks for; the usual term is toothache.
A literal translation of “dolor de muelas”; in English the pain is named with the compound in -ache.

glosario.definicion_l: an ache localized in or around a tooth
causing fear or dread or terror · exceptionally bad or displeasing

ejercicios.frase: I have a ___ throat and I can't speak.
ejercicios.explicacion: The throat is an exception to the -ache rule: you do not say “throatache”, but “a sore throat”, as the table in the card shows. Sore means painful, irritated, and is used with parts of the body that hurt because of inflammation or effort (sore muscles, sore eyes). The clue is the noun throat after the gap and the article a in front.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A pain in the throat is a sore throat.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me duele la garganta y no puedo hablar.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “A pain throat” does not exist; before throat you need the adjective sore.
Hurt is a verb (my throat hurts); as an adjective before the noun, use sore.
Ache is not placed in front as an adjective; also, with the throat the fixed expression is a sore throat.

glosario.definicion_l: hurting · causing misery or pain or distress
the passage to the stomach and lungs; in the front part of the neck below the chin and above the collarbone · an opening in the vamp of a shoe at the instep

ejercicios.frase: My uncle gave ___ smoking ten years ago.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the expression give up smoking from the table, which means to stop a habit. Give up is a phrasal verb: the particle up completely changes the meaning of give. The clue is smoking after the gap: give up is followed by a noun or an -ing gerund (give up smoking, give up sugar), never by to + infinitive.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To stop a habit is give up.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi tío dejó de fumar hace diez años.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Give out means to hand out or to run out; to stop a habit is give up.
Give off means to produce (a smell, smoke); it does not mean to stop smoking.
Give away means to give something for free or to betray someone; to stop a habit is give up.

glosario.definicion_l: lose (something) or lose the right to (something) by some error, offense, or crime · give up with the intent of never claiming again
the brother of your father or mother; the husband of your aunt · a source of help and advice and encouragement

ejercicios.explicacion: The expression in the table is be allergic to: the adjective allergic always takes the preposition to, which here matches Spanish “a”. The clue is the adjective allergic just before the gap. Notice also that nuts has no article because we are talking about nuts in general.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “ser alérgico a” is be allergic to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hijo es alérgico a los frutos secos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Allergic does not take of; the fixed preposition is to.
At is not used with allergic; the correct form is allergic to.
With is not the preposition for allergic; the correct one is to.

glosario.definicion_l: informal or slang terms for mentally irregular

ejercicios.frase: I need to ___ an appointment with the dentist.
ejercicios.explicacion: The collocation in the table is make an appointment, to arrange an appointment. In English appointment goes with make, not with do or take, and it is worth memorising as a chunk. The clue is the noun appointment just after the gap. When you already have the appointment, you say have an appointment.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To arrange an appointment is make an appointment.
ejercicios.traduccion: Necesito pedir cita con el dentista.

por_opcion.make: Correct: make an appointment means to arrange an appointment.
por_opcion.do: Incorrect: do is used with tasks and activities (do homework), not with appointment.
por_opcion.take: Incorrect: take an appointment is a literal translation; in English the natural collocation is make.

glosario.definicion_l: a person qualified to practice dentistry

ejercicios.frase: You can't buy these pills without a ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The doctor's written order, the document the doctor signs so you can buy a medicine, is a prescription, as the table shows. The clue is the context of the pills. The other options are typical traps caused by Spanish “receta” or by words with a similar form.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The doctor's written order is a prescription.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puedes comprar estas pastillas sin receta.

por_opcion.prescription: Correct: the doctor's written order for medicine.
por_opcion.recipe: Incorrect: recipe is a cooking recipe (a recipe for paella).
por_opcion.receipt: Incorrect: receipt is the piece of paper you get when you buy something.

glosario.definicion_l: available only with a doctor's written prescription · directions prescribed beforehand; the action of prescribing authoritative rules or directions
something that resembles a tablet of medicine in shape or size · a dose of medicine in the form of a small pellet

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the fixed formula from the table What's the matter?, equivalent to Spanish “¿Qué te pasa?”. It is used when you see that someone is not well (the clue is You look pale). Matter here means “problem, issue”, and if you want to be more specific you add with: What's the matter with you?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “¿Qué te pasa?” is What's the matter?

por_opcion.matter: Correct: What's the matter? is the fixed question for Spanish “¿Qué te pasa?”.
por_opcion.problem with you: Incorrect: “What's the problem with you?” sounds aggressive, like “What's your problem?”; it is not the friendly formula to show concern.
por_opcion.thing: Incorrect: “What's the thing?” is not a natural expression in English.

glosario.definicion_l: very light colored; highly diluted with white · (of light) lacking in intensity or brightness; dim or feeble

ejercicios.frase: I fell off my bike and ___ my knee.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes hurt meaning “to cause pain, to injure yourself”: hurt + part of the body means to injure that part (I hurt my knee). The clue is that there is a direct object, my knee, and a cause, the fall. Hurt is irregular and its past is the same as the infinitive: hurt. Also, the possessive my is used, not the article.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To injure a part of the body is hurt + part of the body.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me caí de la bici y me hice daño en la rodilla.

por_opcion.hurt: Correct: hurt my knee, to injure your knee; irregular past, the same as the present.
por_opcion.ached: Incorrect: ache is intransitive (my knee ached) and takes no direct object.
por_opcion.pained: Incorrect: pain as a verb is rare and means to sadden; it is not used for injuring yourself.

glosario.definicion_l: suffering from physical injury especially that suffered in battle · damaged; used of inanimate objects or their value
come off · fall heavily or suddenly; decline markedly
hinge joint in the human leg connecting the tibia and fibula with the femur and protected in front by the patella · joint between the femur and tibia in a quadruped; corresponds to the human knee

ejercicios.frase: I'm constipated: I'm sneezing and I have a runny nose.
respuestas: I've got a cold: I'm sneezing and I have a runny nose.
I have a cold: I'm sneezing and I have a runny nose.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the false friend pointed out in Rules and key points: constipated means “estreñido”, not “constipado”. A cold is a cold, and you say I have a cold or I've got a cold. The clue is the symptoms: sneezing and a runny nose, typical of a cold. Both forms, have and have got, are accepted because both express possession in British English.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “constipado” (with a cold) is have a cold; constipated means “estreñido”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estoy resfriado: estornudo y me moquea la nariz.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm constipated: I'm sneezing and I have a runny nose.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: constipated means “estreñido”, so the message is absurd.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have cold: I'm sneezing and I have a runny nose.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The article is missing: a cold.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm cold: I'm sneezing and I have a runny nose.
errores_previstos.explicacion: I'm cold means you feel cold, not that you have a cold.

glosario.definicion_l: impede with a clog or as if with a clog · cause to be constipated
a symptom consisting of the involuntary expulsion of air from the nose · exhale spasmodically, as when an irritant entered one's nose

ejercicios.frase: She broke the arm playing basketball.
respuestas: She broke her arm playing basketball.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card: with parts of the body, English uses the possessive, not the article. Where Spanish says “se rompió el brazo”, English says “she broke her arm”. The clue is the subject she, which requires the possessive her. Using the sounds as if she broke someone else's arm or the arm of an object.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With parts of the body, use the possessive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Se rompió el brazo jugando al baloncesto.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She broke the arm playing basketball.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: with parts of the body, use the possessive, her arm.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She broke his arm playing basketball.
errores_previstos.explicacion: His is the masculine possessive: it would mean she broke a boy's arm. With she, use her.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She broke herself the arm playing basketball.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A literal translation of the Spanish reflexive “se rompió”; English has no reflexive here, the possessive is enough: her arm.

glosario.definicion_l: a game played on a court by two opposing teams of 5 players; points are scored by throwing the ball through an elevated horizontal hoop · an inflated ball used in playing basketball

ejercicios.frase: I have a pain of head.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for pains: Spanish “dolor de cabeza” is headache, with the article a (I have a headache). The original sentence is a word-for-word translation from Spanish. Three solutions are accepted because the card gives two ways of expressing pain: have (got) + a + compound in -ache, or part of the body + hurts (my head hurts).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Pain in the head is headache.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have a pain of head.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: “pain of head” is a literal translation; the word is headache.
Headache is countable and takes an article: a headache.
A literal translation of Spanish “me duele”: here hurt takes no personal object; my head hurts is enough.

glosario.definicion_l: something or someone that causes anxiety; a source of unhappiness · pain in the head caused by dilation of cerebral arteries or muscle contractions or a reaction to drugs
suffering from physical injury especially that suffered in battle · damaged; used of inanimate objects or their value

respuestas: I hope you get better soon
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the fixed formula for wishing someone a quick recovery, with get better (to improve) from the table. The order is a main clause (I hope) plus a subordinate clause without that (you get better), with the adverb soon at the end. Notice that after hope English uses the present simple, where Spanish uses the subjunctive (“que te mejores”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Formula for wishing someone a quick recovery.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I hope you get soon better
errores_previstos.explicacion: Soon cannot separate get from better, which form a unit (get better); the adverb goes at the end: get better soon.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I hope get you better soon
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject you must go before the verb get.

glosario.definicion_l: United States comedian (born in England) who appeared in films with Bing Crosby (1903-2003) · a specific instance of feeling hopeful

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the expression from the table keep fit, to stay in good physical condition. Purpose is expressed with to + infinitive (to keep fit), where Spanish says “para”. The order is subject + main verb (I swim) + purpose. You do not say “for keep fit”: to express the purpose of an action, use to. The purpose can also go first: To keep fit, I swim.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Keep fit means to stay in good physical condition.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It reverses the relationship: it would mean you keep fit so that you can swim.
Keep fit is a fixed expression with the verb first: to keep fit.

glosario.definicion_l: the act of swimming · travel through water

ejercicios.frase: Take his temperature; I think he has a ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes a temperature meaning a high body temperature: have a temperature means to have a fever, not simply to have a temperature. Have a fever is also accepted; it is more common in American English. The clue is the article a before the gap and the context of taking someone's temperature. Both answers are correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To have a high body temperature is have a temperature or have a fever.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tómale la temperatura; creo que tiene fiebre.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the Spanish word; in English you say fever or temperature.
Hot is an adjective; after a you need a noun: a temperature or a fever.

glosario.definicion_l: a rise in the temperature of the body; frequently a symptom of infection · a state of nervous excitement

ejercicios.frase: I stood up too quickly and felt ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes feel dizzy, to feel as if everything is spinning. It is what happens when you stand up suddenly (the clue is stood up too quickly). Feel is followed by an adjective that describes how you feel, and dizzy is the one for the feeling that everything is going round.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me levanté demasiado deprisa y me mareé.

por_opcion.dizzy: Correct: feeling that everything is spinning.
por_opcion.sore: Incorrect: sore means painful and applies to a part of the body (a sore throat), not to how you feel in general.
por_opcion.allergic: Incorrect: allergic takes to; it does not describe feeling dizzy.

glosario.definicion_l: rise to one's feet · refuse to back down; remain solid under criticism or attack

descripcion_larga_es: Basic vocabulary for talking about health: parts of the body, pains and symptoms, the doctor's surgery, the chemist's and healthy habits. It is essential when travelling and in daily life, because in an emergency you need to explain yourself quickly and clearly. It is difficult for Spanish speakers because of several false friends (constipated, recipe, sick) and because English uses the possessive with parts of the body.

contexto.que_es: It is basic health vocabulary: the body (head, back, knee), pains (headache, a sore throat), common illnesses (a cold, the flu), verbs for injuring yourself (hurt, injure) and expressions used at the doctor's (make an appointment, prescription). It also includes lifestyle habits (keep fit, give up smoking).
contexto.por_que_importa: It is one of the most useful areas in real situations: when travelling, at the doctor's or at the chemist's you need to say exactly what is wrong. A false friend can cause serious or comic misunderstandings: saying “I'm constipated” when you have a cold means something very different. In basic-level exams it is a classic topic for conversation and writing.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When making an appointment, describing symptoms to the doctor or the pharmacist, asking someone what is wrong (What's the matter?) or wishing them a quick recovery. The signals are verbs of pain and parts of the body. Spanish speakers tend to say “the arm” instead of “my arm”, “pain of head” for “headache” and “recipe” for “prescription”.
